title: Adobe vs. International Business Machines: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
detail:
Adobe vs. International Business Machines: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Sara Appino, The Motley Fool

ADBE
IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Choosing between a creative software titan and an enterprise infrastructure legend depends on your financial goals. Deciding between Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) and International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) requires a close look at their growth and stability profiles.

Adobe leads the market in design and document workflows, moving aggressively into generative artificial intelligence. IBM focuses on the backbone of corporate technology, specializing in hybrid cloud and consulting. While both serve the enterprise sector, they offer distinct financial profiles, making this a choice between high-margin software and steady, global infrastructure.

The case for Adobe

Adobe develops an end-to-end platform for creative, productivity, and marketing workflows. Its solutions serve business professionals, consumers, and large enterprise marketing teams in the tech stocks market. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company highlighted how it integrates third-party platforms to support its content supply chain and generative AI models. It also expanded its capabilities through the acquisition of Topaz Labs L.L.C. in June 2026.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $23.8 billion, which was an increase of approximately 10.5% over the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $7.1 billion, up from approximately $5.6 billion in FY 2024. This performance led to a net margin of roughly 30%, representing the percentage of total sales remaining after all business expenses are paid. Management noted that growth was consistent across its creative and document cloud segments.

As of its November 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.6x, meaning for every dollar of equity held by shareholders, the company has 60 cents in total debt. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, was approximately 1.0x. Free cash flow, defined as cash from operations minus capital expenditures, reached close to $9.9 billion. This strong cash generation allows the company to reinvest in its AI-powered product roadmap.

The case for International Business Machines

International Business Machines focuses on providing hybrid cloud and AI-driven technology solutions for digital transformation. The company serves clients across a vast array of industries, including financial services, healthcare, and retail. It maintains a broad ecosystem of strategic partners, including Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ:PANW), Salesforce (NYSE:CRM), Samsung Electronics (OTC:SSNLF), and SAP (NYSE:SAP). These collaborations allow the company to deliver end-to-end solutions for complex business challenges.

Cash Flow Covers the Dividend More Than Twice

In 2025, IBM produced $14.73 billion of free cash flow and paid $6.255 billion in common dividends. That covered the dividend about 2.4 times. On the October 21 call, CFO Jim Kavanaugh gave the 2026 picture so far:

"Through the first nine months, we generated about $8 billion of free cash flow, up 8% year-over-year."

IBM, he said, "returned $4.8 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends through the first nine months of the year." That puts coverage near 1.7 times with the fourth quarter still ahead. Management also expects full-year free cash flow to grow by more than $1 billion.

Where the Dividend Cash Comes From

Most of IBM's cash comes from recurring revenue. Clients pay year after year for Red Hat software, data tools, and the mainframe software that runs banks and airlines. title: IBM’s Software Business Is Picking Up Speed. Here’s Why It’s Time to Grab IBM Stock on the Dip.

IBM’s Software Business Is Picking Up Speed. Here’s Why It’s Time to Grab IBM Stock on the Dip.
Sushree Mohanty
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 10:31 AM EDT 5 min read
IBM
Trade IBM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
A corporate office for IBM by HJBC via Adobe Stock

International Business Machines (IBM) has spent the last couple of years trying to convince investors it's more than an old-school technology giant. A quarter ago, IBM's software story looked less comfortable, with delayed deals and timing issues clouding the outlook. The third quarter brought better news as the software business accelerated, showing strength across key areas, including Red Hat and data software.

Yet, IBM shares remain well below their $332.46 peak and are down 14% so far this year. If this momentum continues into the coming quarters, investors buying the dip could enter before the market fully recognizes the improvement in IBM's software business.

A Beaten-Down Stock Meets a Better Earnings Story

Trouble began brewing as IBM's software business lost momentum. Software revenue climbed just 5% year-over-year (YoY) in the second quarter, down sharply from 11% in the first quarter and 14% in the fourth quarter of 2025. The slowdown was upsetting because software has been central to IBM's transformation beyond its legacy hardware business. Investors had counted on this segment to drive stronger growth, so the disappointing numbers hurt confidence in the strategy. Management pointed to the company's failure to close several large software deals on schedule, leading to a delay in recognizing revenue. Yet lingering uncertainty about when that missing revenue might arrive continued to drag on the stock.

The third quarter gave a more encouraging picture. IBM generated $17.1 billion in revenue, up 5% YoY. Software revenue reached $7.8 billion, increasing 8% over the year-ago quarter and accounting for roughly 46% of total revenue. Adjusted earnings per share rose 11% to $2.95 from the year-ago quarter. During the Q3 earnings call, management stressed that software growth rose by four percentage points to reach 9% in the third quarter, backed by IBM's robust recurring-revenue base and sharper deal execution. CFO Jim Kavanaugh noted that three of four software sub-segments posted strong double-digit revenue gains, driven by a wave of new business and more effective pipeline conversion. IBM also won about two-thirds of the major deals it had missed in the second quarter. This mix of new wins and reclaimed contracts signals a rebound that goes beyond timing, pointing to deeper, more sustained momentum.

title: The Open Question Under IBM Stock
detail:
The Open Question Under IBM Stock

International Business Machines (IBM) sells large companies the work of putting AI to use. Management credits client demand for that work with the growth in its consulting business. The risk is that those clients grow wary of what their AI spending returns and cut back. You cannot yet tell whether that wariness has started to reach IBM's sales.

Where IBM Would Feel A Pullback In AI Spending

The place to look is IBM's consulting business. Management said consulting revenue grew 2% in the third quarter of 2026, excluding currency moves, reflecting continued client demand for AI-enabled transformation. Management has also said larger enterprises are becoming much more aware of the true return on their AI spending, and that some worry part of it has run out of control with no real return. The spending that management credits for consulting's growth is the same spending clients are now looking at harder.

Analysts are asking about it. On IBM's October 21, 2026 call, eight analysts asked questions, and three of them asked about AI. One of them raised the doubt directly, asking whether clients had held back on deals after finding that some AI systems could not do what was claimed for them.

How Big Is IBM's Consulting Business?

Consulting brought in $21.1 billion in fiscal 2025, about 31% of IBM's total revenue that year. Only Software was larger, at $30.0 billion. Consulting revenue grew 1.8% in fiscal 2025, after a 0.9% fall in fiscal 2024. That is far slower than Software, which grew 10.6% that year. These yearly figures are as reported in IBM's annual filings, unlike the third-quarter rise above. A pullback in clients' AI spending would hit the AI work within consulting. Consulting is nearly a third of IBM's sales, and it is a business that has only just returned to growth.

Has IBM's Management Answered The Doubts On AI?

Management has answered in part. It said that the productivity gains from AI are very real, and that a lot of people underplay how much work it takes to fit AI into their workflows. That work is the kind of AI-enabled transformation management credits for consulting's growth.

On the October 21 call after the third quarter, management said it expects consulting revenue growth to pick up to low to mid-single digits for 2026, citing backlog quality and momentum in GenAI. Asked about software, management said it did not want to comment on 2027 growth yet. It said it would quantify its early thinking on software and IBM as a whole in January. Until then, consulting revenue growth, against that guide of low to mid-single digits for 2026, is the number to watch in IBM's next report, expected in January 2027.
